claims.text: Depositing a nanostructured adaptive tribo-ceramic coating on a high-entropy alloy will reduce both friction and wear.
The coating will form a self-adjusting lubricious tribolayer in situ during operation.
The untreated high-entropy alloy has variable friction and wear performance across temperature extremes.
Physical vapor deposition can produce the proposed nanostructured adaptive tribo-ceramic coating on the alloy.
The proposed operating window extends from approximately -50°C to 800°C under sliding or rolling contact and varying loads and speeds.
The coating's nanostructured ceramic phase transforms into an adaptive lubricious oxide or mixed-ceramic surface layer.
Sliding induces localized tribo-oxidation and phase transformation in the coating.
The tribolayer is ultra-thin and self-adjusting.
The oxide or ceramic tribolayer reduces direct contact between the coated surface and the counterface.
The tribolayer provides an easily sheared, lower-shear-strength interface.
Reduced direct contact and interfacial shear lower both coefficient of friction and wear rate.
Prior studies observed beneficial lubricating oxide layers under high load and with particular compositional features.
The coated alloy will have lower friction and wear than the untreated alloy over the full -50°C to 800°C service-temperature range.
Friction and wear may be reduced by approximately 20–30% or more under typical operating conditions.
Temperature-dependent oxide formation and microstructural instability cause variability in the untreated alloy's friction and wear.
The coating will remain effective if it adheres well, retains its nanostructure, and avoids degradation from thermal cycling or excessive chemical reaction.
The magnitude of improvement and long-term tribolayer stability under repeated sliding and extreme thermal cycling are uncertain.
Failure to obtain consistently lower friction and wear than the untreated control at all tested temperatures, or failure to form a stable tribolayer, would falsify the hypothesis.
